focus: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

items.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
items.source: Kwon et al., UC Berkeley (SOSP 2023, vLLM)
items.why: LLM serving is a memory-management problem before it is a compute problem. This paper is the clearest example of applying classic OS ideas (paging, copy-on-write, preemption) to a new workload, and it is the foundation for understanding every modern inference engine.
items.summary:
The KV cache of a request is large (roughly 800 KB per token for OPT-13B), grows by one token per step, and has unknown final length. Prior systems stored it as one contiguous tensor sized for the maximum length, which wastes memory three ways: reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation, and external fragmentation. The paper measures that only about 20 to 38 percent of KV memory held real token state in those systems, which caps batch size and therefore throughput.

PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens) that need not be contiguous in GPU memory. A per-request block table maps logical blocks to physical blocks, exactly like a page table, and blocks are allocated on demand so waste is bounded to the last partially filled block. The attention kernel is rewritten to gather keys and values block by block, computing scores per block and a softmax across all of them.

Because mapping is indirect, sharing becomes cheap. Parallel sampling and beam search share prompt blocks through reference counts, and a write to a shared block triggers copy-on-write of just that one block. Shared system prompts work the same way. Beam search savings in memory reach 40 to 66 percent in their experiments.

Scheduling is FCFS with continuous (iteration-level) batching. When GPU blocks run out, the latest requests are preempted all-or-nothing per sequence group, either by swapping blocks to CPU memory or by recomputing the KV from the prompt plus generated tokens. Recompute is attractive at small block sizes because small PCIe transfers underuse bandwidth. Block size is a tradeoff between kernel parallelism and table overhead on the small side and internal fragmentation and reduced sharing on the large side. Reported result: 2 to 4x throughput over FasterTransformer and Orca at equal latency, with no change to model outputs; the paged attention kernel itself is 20 to 26 percent slower than a contiguous one, which the batch size gain more than pays for.
items.exercise: In Python with numpy, build a toy paged KV cache: a physical block pool, a per-sequence block table, an allocator with free list, and refcounted fork with copy-on-write. Implement single-head attention that gathers over blocks and verify it matches attention over a contiguous cache to 1e-6. Then simulate a Poisson stream of requests with random output lengths and plot achievable batch size for contiguous max-length allocation versus paged allocation.

items.title: The Internals of PostgreSQL, Chapter 5: Concurrency Control
items.why: Snapshot isolation, visibility rules and txid wraparound explain a large share of real-world Postgres behavior: bloat, vacuum pressure, write skew, and serialization failures. The same mental model transfers to any MVCC engine.
items.summary:
PostgreSQL implements MVCC as snapshot isolation by writing new row versions directly into the heap page, rather than into rollback segments as Oracle does. Each tuple header carries t_xmin (inserting txid), t_xmax (deleting or updating txid, zero if none, also reused for row locks), t_cid (command counter within the transaction), and t_ctid (pointer to itself or to the newer version after an update).

Transaction status lives in the commit log, logically an array indexed by txid with four states: in progress, committed, aborted, sub-committed. A snapshot is the triple xmin:xmax:xip_list: the oldest still-active txid, the first unassigned txid, and the list of active txids in between. Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read and Serializable take one at the first statement.

Visibility is a decision procedure over t_xmin and t_xmax status plus the snapshot. An aborted inserter means invisible. A committed inserter that is still in the snapshot's active list is invisible. A tuple is visible unless there is a deleter that committed and is not in the active list. The chapter walks through ten explicit rules, including the cases where the current transaction itself inserted or deleted the tuple.

Postgres Repeatable Read is true snapshot isolation (no phantoms) but permits write skew. Serializable uses SSI, added in 9.1: it records reads as SIREAD predicate locks at tuple, page and relation granularity, detects rw-conflicts on writes, and aborts on a dangerous structure of two consecutive rw edges, first committer winning. It can give false positives (sequential scans lock the whole relation) but never false negatives.

Maintenance closes the loop. Txids are 32-bit and compared circularly, so a tuple older than about 2.1 billion transactions would suddenly look like it is from the future. Freezing marks old tuples as always visible (since 9.4 via a hint bit in t_infomask instead of rewriting t_xmin), and vacuum also removes dead tuples, trims the commit log, and updates the free space and visibility maps.
items.exercise: Spin up Postgres in Docker. Use pageinspect (heap_page_items) and the xmin, xmax, ctid system columns to watch versions appear across INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in two concurrent sessions. Then reproduce write skew (two doctors on call) under REPEATABLE READ and show it aborts with SQLSTATE 40001 under SERIALIZABLE. Finally write a small C# or Python function implementing the ten visibility rules over (xmin status, xmax status, snapshot) and cross-check it against pg_visible results on a handful of tuples.

items.title: Efficient IO with io_uring
items.why: io_uring is the design that finally made Linux async IO general, and the shared-memory ring pattern with its barrier discipline appears everywhere in high-performance systems, from NIC drivers to database engines. It is also a compact lesson in lock-free SPSC queue design.
items.summary:
The design replaces the awkward native aio interface, which only handled O_DIRECT, could still block on submission, copied 64 plus 8 bytes per submission and 32 per completion, and needed at least two syscalls per operation. io_uring instead maps two rings into shared memory between application and kernel: a submission queue and a completion queue. No per-operation copy happens, and each ring is single-producer single-consumer so no locks are required.

Ring indices are free-running 32-bit counters masked by ring size (a power of two), which removes the need for a separate full flag. For submission, the application fills an SQE (opcode, flags, fd, offset, address, length, user_data, padded to 64 bytes), writes its index into the SQ index array, issues a write barrier, then publishes the new tail. The kernel reads the tail after a read barrier. For completion, the kernel is the sole writer of CQEs and the CQ tail, and the application owns the CQ head. A CQE carries only user_data and a result code, and completions can arrive in any order.

The separate SQE array behind an index array lets applications embed SQEs in their own structures and submit them in any order. Because the kernel copies what it needs at submission, in-flight requests can exceed SQ size. io_uring_enter combines submit and wait in one syscall, and with SQPOLL a kernel thread polls the SQ so steady-state submission needs no syscall at all (it sleeps after idle time and the app must wake it via a flag check).

Further savings come from registration: fixed files avoid atomic refcount traffic on every operation, and fixed buffers avoid repeated page pinning and mapping for O_DIRECT. Linked SQEs express dependencies (a failure or short transfer cancels the rest of the chain with ECANCELED), and drain is a heavier barrier that stalls the whole queue. The article reports roughly 1.7M 4k IOPS polled versus about 608K for aio on its test hardware, which should be read as relative, not current, numbers.
items.exercise: In C with liburing (or Rust with the io-uring crate), write a file copier that keeps 32 reads in flight with a registered buffer pool, chains each read to a write using IOSQE_IO_LINK, and measure throughput against a plain read/write loop and a thread-pool version on a large file. Then drop liburing and implement the raw ring protocol with mmap and explicit acquire/release atomics for one NOP-submit and reap loop to see the barrier rules concretely.

items.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft, extended version)
items.source: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, Stanford
items.why: Raft is the consensus algorithm behind etcd, Consul, CockroachDB and many others. Knowing exactly why each rule exists, especially the commit rule for previous-term entries, is what separates using a replicated log from being able to debug one.
items.summary:
Time is divided into terms, numbered consecutively, each beginning with an election. Terms act as a logical clock: any server seeing a higher term adopts it and reverts to follower, and any request with a stale term is rejected. Persistent state per server is currentTerm, votedFor and the log, flushed before replying to RPCs.

Followers that hear nothing for a randomized election timeout (for example 150 to 300 ms) become candidates, increment the term, vote for themselves and send RequestVote in parallel. Randomization makes split votes rare and resolves them quickly, which the authors preferred over a ranking scheme that had awkward corner cases. A vote is granted only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as the voter's, compared by last entry term and then by length. This election restriction guarantees any new leader already holds every committed entry.

Replication uses AppendEntries carrying prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm. A follower rejects if its log has no matching entry there, which by induction yields the Log Matching property: same index and term means identical prefixes. The leader tracks nextIndex per follower and backs up on rejection, so the leader's log overwrites divergent follower suffixes while the leader never alters its own log. Followers advance commitIndex to min(leaderCommit, last new entry).

The subtle part is Figure 8: a leader must not count replicas to commit an entry from an earlier term, because a majority-replicated old entry can still be overwritten by a later leader elected with a log that lacks it. Leaders therefore commit only entries from their current term by counting, and earlier entries become committed indirectly through Log Matching. Membership changes use joint consensus, where a combined configuration requires separate majorities from both old and new sets before switching, avoiding two disjoint majorities in the same term. (Note: the joint consensus section was read via a summary, so check the paper for exact details.)
items.exercise: Implement Raft leader election and log replication (no snapshots or membership change) in C# or Go over an in-memory simulated network with controllable message drops, delays and partitions. Encode the five safety properties as assertions and run a randomized fault-injection test for a few thousand steps. Then deliberately remove the current-term check from the commit rule and reproduce the Figure 8 scenario with a scripted schedule to see the safety violation yourself.
